messages.body_plain:
On 9/1/13 5:45 PM, Ross Boylan wrote:
> Some .hpp files look more like .cpp files in that they have a lot of
> implementation code in them, e.g., stanc_helper.hpp.  Is there a reason
> for that?

Yes and no.

With template classes and functions, there's not a clean way
to separate headers and implementations.  There's a great
discussion in Vandevoorde and Josuttis's book on C++ Templates (really
THE book on template programming in C++).

If you look at Eigen and Boost, the libs on which we're based,
you'll see they're almost exclusively header only.  This means there
are NO implementation files, just header files.

> It may not make any practical difference (though it may explain some of
> the long compile times), but I'm just trying to understand what's going
> on.

The long compile times are from all the template metaprogramming
and evaluation going on in Eigen and in our auto-diff lib.

> One possible rationale is that the files are going into an include
> directory, at least for rstan.  But there are already a bunch of .cpp
> files that go there, so that doesn't seem to be it.
>
> Some C++ compilers might also react badly to having the same code
> compiled in more than one place.

You have to be careful to only ever compile a definition in a single
translation unit.

Now having said all this, Vandevoorde and Josuttis also show you how
to divide the code up so that you have three kinds of files:

    foo.hpp       (headers only)
    foo_def.hpp   (headers with defs)
    foo_inst.cpp  (instantiations)

This way you strip the headers down to just headers with only
declarations and no function definitions.  The _def.hpp is what
you see in header-only template libs.  You can include those and
use them header only and ignore the _inst.cpp files.

Then _inst.cpp has instantiations, which says
which instantiations of the templates to compile into object code.
You can compile these ahead of time and then use the headers .hpp
files, but only for instantiations of templates you prespecified in
_inst.cpp.

The plan is to move more of Stan to this style of code, but we
have a big problem in that some of our template instantation patterns
are huge.  For instance, the Student-t distribution function has
hundreds of instantiations (vectorization plus auto-diff inside
the arg structure with free choices leading to horrible combinatorics).

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: MCSim as a model of how to do ode in Stan
messages.subject_clean: MCSim as a model of how to do ode in Stan
messages.body_plain:
In the hopes that my experience with MCSim might help with Stan's implementation of an ODE solver, I'll post a few ideas.

First: why have I used MCSim?  It's probably for a somewhat different reason than most.  I’ve used MCSim as a system dynamics simulator in the spirit of John Sterman’s Business Dynamics and of the System Dynamics Society (http://www.systemdynamics.org/whatisSD/). In essence, this is classical feedback control theory applied to human, organizational, and environmental systems.

>From a modeling perspective, these models are characterized by systems of equations, usually expressed in integral rather than differential form for philosophical reasons, and with frequent tabular nonlinearities. Higher-end simulators make use of Kalman filtering and optimization to extract signals out of noisy data and to adjust parameters to best achieve certain goals.
Before encountering MCSim, I had created such models using iThink (isee systems), Vensim, and homebrew solutions written in Logo, Pascal, and C (built on the SimPack framework).

You can see a short example system dynamics model in MCSim in the quick reference guide at http://www.gnu.org/software/mcsim/.

What worked well in MCSim?

I’ve enjoyed working in MCSim, and I trust Frederic’s approach to crafting an expressive language for describing ODEs. Two key things impressed me about MCSim as compared to commercial simulators:

- the presence of automated solvers that eliminated the need to specify dt (you still needed to specify “stiff,” if that characterized the equations)
- that something about MCSim led me naturally to designed experiments instead of OFAT experiments on models from the very beginning

I think I was led to DOE because the models were in text, not drawn graphically, and because the model and the knowns (data and parameters) and the experiments were prespecified in separate locations.

In the hopes that these capabilities remain in the Stan ODE solver, here are a few other things I found useful.

1. the expressiveness of the language (I didn’t really miss the integral form)
2. the ability to choose one’s solver
3. thanks to deSolve, the ability to handle events (although I have yet to use them)
4. The ability to handle tabular nonlinearities with arbitrary interpolation routines using the GSL or one’s own code
5. That models were compiled and could be executed rapidly with new data without recompiling
6. that there was an xmcsim for quick prototyping, even as I only used it rarely.

I recognize that it’s unlikely for Stan to be compatible with the GSL; perhaps Boost offers similar productivity in its interpolation capabilities.  I’ve tended to use Akima interpolation because it can handle arbitrarily-spaced input resolution as well as step and linear interpolation to be compatible with commercial simulators.  I use Stineman interpolation in some cases, although I can’t think of a case where I used that in a system dynamics model.

There were things that were awkward in MCSim.

In order to facilitate tabular nonlinearities, Frederic implemented inline sections. The naming of variables became a bit arcane, as you would need different names for the same variable, depending upon whether it was in the model or the inline code.

There was no easy ability to organize equations into submodels.

As I recall (it’s been a couple of years since I’ve used MCSim regularly), MCSim’s output had two formats. I suspect most of us used R to visualize the data, it might have been handy to have standard interface routines to facilitate moving the data into a data frame (I suspect Frederic and everyone else using it developed their own.  It was easy to grab the data in gnuplot.

I generally liked MCSim’s model structure, which seems similar to that chosen for Stan.  Still, most of the commercial system dynamics simulators sort the equations automatically, so you can write them in the order that makes sense to people, and the simulator reorders them so that variables are calculated in the order needed.  For example, in other systems, you can order the differential equations and their supporting equations in ways that make sense to people without worrying about being sure that variables have valid values when their defining equation is executed.  Perhaps something could be done with tangle inside an orgmode file that contains R and Stan code, but that still sounds manual.

Ask if something isn't clear.  These are quick ideas based on my experience; there are no doubt better ways to do things.  I just wanted to make sure we didn't lose the ability to do system-dynamic-type models in Stan, too.

Bill

this will rub off on our design.

On 9/7/13 1:38 AM, Bill Harris wrote:
> In the hopes that my experience with MCSim might help with Stan's implementation of an ODE solver, I'll post a few ideas.
>

> First: why have I used MCSim?  It's probably for a somewhat different reason than most.  Iï¿½ve used MCSim as a system dynamics simulator in the spirit of John Stermanï¿½s Business Dynamics and of the System Dynamics Society (http://www.systemdynamics.org/whatisSD/). In essence, this is classical feedback control theory applied to human, organizational, and environmental systems.

>
>  From a modeling perspective, these models are characterized by systems of equations, usually expressed in integral rather than differential form for philosophical reasons, and with frequent tabular nonlinearities. Higher-end simulators make use of Kalman filtering and optimization to extract signals out of noisy data and to adjust parameters to best achieve certain goals.
> Before encountering MCSim, I had created such models using iThink (isee systems), Vensim, and homebrew solutions written in Logo, Pascal, and C (built on the SimPack framework).
>
> You can see a short example system dynamics model in MCSim in the quick reference guide at http://www.gnu.org/software/mcsim/.

That's exactly what I've been studying.  I like
the basic language.

I think in Stan we're going to need to think of
the ode as producing a function w.r.t parameters
that can be evaluated for output at an array of times.

> What worked well in MCSim?
>

> Iï¿½ve enjoyed working in MCSim, and I trust Fredericï¿½s approach to crafting an expressive language for describing ODEs. Two key things impressed me about MCSim as compared to commercial simulators:
>
> - the presence of automated solvers that eliminated the need to specify dt (you still needed to specify ï¿½stiff,ï¿½ if that characterized the equations)

I'm not sure what this means.  Do you just mean that you don't need
to hand-write the Jacobian for stiff solvers?  That's part of our
plan -- we have the auto-diff tech to do it (it still needs to have
all of our densities implemented for fwd-mode auto-diff before
this is complete).

> - that something about MCSim led me naturally to designed experiments instead of OFAT experiments on models from the very beginning

That's definitely the purpose.  If you ahve something
specific to build, just build that --- you can usually make
it much more efficient.

> I think I was led to DOE because the models were in text, not drawn graphically, and because the model and the knowns (data and parameters) and the experiments were prespecified in separate locations.

Stan puts declarations of both data and parameters
in one place -- the model file.  But data's stored
separately.  And everything's typed.

> In the hopes that these capabilities remain in the Stan ODE solver, here are a few other things I found useful.
>

> 1. the expressiveness of the language (I didnï¿½t really miss the integral form)

I don't even know the integral form --- we were planning on the
diff-eq form.

> 2. the ability to choose oneï¿½s solver

We're hoping to just get one for stiff equations up before
expanding our repertoire, but they'll definitely be plug-and-play
like our samplers and optimizers if we do.

> 3. thanks to deSolve, the ability to handle events (although I have yet to use them)

Not sure what this means.  We're going to have "dosing",
which will allow arbitrary non-continuous shocks to be
added to the system.

> 4. The ability to handle tabular nonlinearities with arbitrary interpolation routines using the GSL or oneï¿½s own code

I'll have to ask Frederic about this.

> 5. That models were compiled and could be executed rapidly with new data without recompiling

This is how Stan works.

> 6. that there was an xmcsim for quick prototyping, even as I only used it rarely.

Don't know this --- I'll take a look.   Is that an interpreter?  I've thought
about doing it for Stan, but we don't have the resources, and our main use
case is for harder models.

> I recognize that itï¿½s unlikely for Stan to be compatible with the GSL;

No.

> perhaps Boost offers similar productivity in its interpolation capabilities.

There are interpolating solvers, but I'm afraid we may have to write
our own because of their lack of templating.  Same conclusion we came
to with Boost's distribution functions.

> Iï¿½ve tended to use Akima interpolation because it can handle arbitrarily-spaced input resolution as well as step and linear interpolation to be compatible with commercial simulators.  I use Stineman interpolation in some cases, although I canï¿½t think of a case where I used that in a system dynamics model.

I hope I understand what this means at some point!

> There were things that were awkward in MCSim.
>
> In order to facilitate tabular nonlinearities, Frederic implemented inline sections. The naming of variables became a bit arcane, as you would need different names for the same variable, depending upon whether it was in the model or the inline code.

We'll use local variables like in computer programs.

> There was no easy ability to organize equations into submodels.

This is something we need to think about for Stan in general.
And these functions for odes are going to be part of a general
way of plugging and re-using functions.

> As I recall (itï¿½s been a couple of years since Iï¿½ve used MCSim regularly), MCSimï¿½s output had two formats. I suspect most of us used R to visualize the data, it might have been handy to have standard interface routines to facilitate moving the data into a data frame (I suspect Frederic and everyone else using it developed their own.  It was easy to grab the data in gnuplot.

Yes --- we do everything in CSV form for command-line operation
and in R's memory when called from R.  I believe we'll be announcing
a really nice Python interface very soon.

> I generally liked MCSimï¿½s model structure, which seems similar to that chosen for Stan.  Still, most of the commercial system dynamics simulators sort the equations automatically, so you can write them in the order that makes sense to people, and the simulator reorders them so that variables are calculated in the order needed.  For example, in other systems, you can order the differential equations and their supporting equations in ways that make sense to people without worrying about being sure that variables have valid values when their defining equation is executed.  Perhaps something could be done with tangle inside an orgmode file that contains R and Stan code, but that still sounds manual.

Things that are not procedural won't be order dependent.  For instance,
you can write sampling statements in any order in a stan model because
the parameters and data are all defined coming into the block.

> Ask if something isn't clear.  These are quick ideas based on my experience; there are no doubt better ways to do things.  I just wanted to make sure we didn't lose the ability to do system-dynamic-type models in Stan, too.

Thanks again.  This is great.

- Bob

I should've been keeping better notes, because Daniel was
driving.  We can send you what we've got so far, which
is nowhere close to compiling.

The stiff solver's more constrained than some of the others
in what it does.  It only works with ublas types (the matrix
lib from Boost).  We might be able to get one of the non-stiff
solvers working.

This is their integrator for stiff systems:

   boost_1.54.0/boost/numeric/odeint/stepper/rosenbrock4.hpp

The over-arching problem is that the assumptions about
(1) initialization and (2) variable lifespan don't play
nicely with reverse-mode auto-dif.

We were getting segfaults everywhere due to (1), though managed
to code around many of those.

The issue with lifespan is that Boost's ublas library for matrices
defines static class constants everywhere by wrapping the scalar type. And
so does the rosenbrock functions.  This won't work with our variable lifespans.
We'd need traits more like those in Eigen, which seem to be modeled on the
function-based approach of std::numeric_limits.  I was sort of surprised
to see Boost using static constants in ublas --- it's usually bad ju-ju in
C++ because of initialization issues.  See:

   /boost/numeric/ublas/matrix.hpp:
   ----------------------------
   ...
   static const value_type one_;

Hmm, now that I just searched for that, I see this in vector:

   boost/numeric/ublas/vector.hpp:
   -------------------------------------
   ...
   typename unit_vector<T, ALLOC>::const_value_type unit_vector<T, ALLOC>::one_ (1);  // ISSUE: need 'one'-traits here

So maybe they're thinking along the same lines.  They should
be calling a one_ function with traits we could specialize,
so that we could use it like +/- infinity or NaN from numeric_limits.

It nearly killed us getting it compiled as far as we did,
but I seem to recall other issues with the time type and
its interaction with the scalar type not doing the right thing.

That and one of the packages trying to use a nullary-constructed
object in some place and segfaulting.  (I think we may have
coded around that, too.)

> http://www.boost.org/doc/libs/1_54_0/libs/numeric/odeint/doc/html/boost_numeric_odeint/tutorial/using_arbitrary_precision_floating_point_types.html

We were following this and the other clues in the doc, some of
which don't apply to Rosenbrock, because it's a special, limited
instance of their interface.

> So, I don't immediately see what additional templating is needed to utilize our types.

I can send you what we have and you can see what we've
done so far.  I don't see how we can get further without further
changing their code, at which point, we'll have rewritten a lot of it.

The Rosenbrock version doesn't look too complicated to reimplement
starting from the Boost impl, and we can swap out the matrix algebra
from UBLAS with Eigen, which we already have working.

- Bob

I've been eating our dogfood a lot recently and this inevitably
brought me back to Andrew's perspective on timing chains.  And it
makes me think we should run many more shorter chains given how
quickly Stan converges.

So how about this:

1. for (chain in 1:NUM_CHAINS) asynchronously [ideally in parallel]

      a.  run adaptation for chain for a fixed time t_a,

      b.  run sampling for chain for a fixed time t_s, and

2.  merge the results with our jagged R-hat and n_eff.

Is there any reason this wouldn't preserve detailed balance?

Which version of jagged R-hat/n_eff to use, the one that weights
by chain or the one that weights by number of samples?  The latter
would seem to be more robust in the face of stuck chains.

Running lots of chains means that each stuck chain contributes
less to the overall total.  If we run 32 chains of length 100
instead of 4 chains of length 800, we get the same number of
samples.  But with 32 chains, the stuck ones should wash out
in the R-hat and n_eff calcs, assuming they're stuck somewhere
near high posterior mass.

- Bob

I'm not sure about this.  I've usually thought that 4 or so chains should suffice.  My reasoning was that we can't really verify mixing until the chains have done about 50 tours each, at which point we have something like 20 independent draws, which is good enough for usual purposes.  If I wanted more draws, I'd run longer, on the theory that then the chains would explore the space further.
On the other hand, here you're talking about problems of stuck chains, and that's another story.  It does seem like we need a general way to handle this problem.
A

messages.body_plain:
It's for robustness.

Is there an argument for 4?  It seems like if you're
hunting for modes on init, you'd want a lot.  Or if
you're looking for tails with low transition probabilities,
you'd want to run a long time.

With only 4, you do need a lot of back and forth movement
to conclude you've converged.  My hope was that we'd need
less with more chains.

I think we get good convergence in most problems after 10
or 20 iterations --- some have taken up to 100 or 200.  After
that, the fast to converge ones mix really well, often
near an effective sample per draw.  Others not so much, with
more like 100 draws per effective sample.  If we then want
100 effective samples, that's 10K iterations, and we can do them
with 30 chains of 3 samples each or fewer longer chains.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
Firstly -- let's forget about finding modes.  HMC is never going to be good at transitioning between nodes even if we can find them.

Consequently the main advantage of multiple starting points is to ensure that either our adaptation hasn't gone awry or we're not missing parts of the distribution with significantly different curvature (for example, the triangle or the Cauchy).  I would argue that most of the problems we're seeing are due to bad adaptation and the multiple starting point is doing exactly what it should.  In particular, I really like how the combined approach of putting more thought into the initializations and choosing better priors has proved so useful.  Better models for a better tomorrow!

On the other hand, if we really do have a model with very different curvature (again, think triangle or Cauchy) then running with many small chains and ignoring those with small ESS can hide that fact and the false belief that everything is automatic could lead to bias.

Personally I think the best way forward is to improve the adaption.  The first easy fix is to add a period of adaptation-free warmup (which I've been playing with on and off since coming to London but just haven't had time to run significant tests).  Then, once the higher-order autodiff is ready, we can starting using a running average of the SoftAbs metric instead of estimating the global covariance.

the motivations for using R-hat.  If different chains are
stuck in different modes, there's not mixing.

choose an init point and get stuck.

Sure, but making any suggestion that we can find all modes, or even some modes, by trying lots of different initialization values is a bit of a false flag.  Once you're trying to deal with mode finding you really want a global, compressive algorithm like nested sampling (perhaps tempering or annealing if you have a particularly well-behaved model) and not a local algorithm like MCMC.

>> Consequently the main advantage of multiple starting points is to ensure that either our adaptation hasn't gone awry or we're not missing parts of the distribution with significantly different curvature (for example, the triangle or the Cauchy).  I would argue that most of the problems we're seeing are due to bad adaptation and the multiple starting point is doing exactly what it should.  In particular, I really like how the combined approach of putting more thought into the initializations and choosing better priors has proved so useful.  Better models for a better tomorrow!
>>
>> On the other hand, if we really do have a model with very different curvature (again, think triangle or Cauchy) then running with many small chains and ignoring those with small ESS can hide that fact and the false belief that everything is automatic could lead to bias.
>
> This is what I'm worried about.  We get the same problem if we don't
> choose an init point and get stuck.

Right, but it's easier to diagnose if we run a few chains for a while.  My concern with lots of little chains is that there'd be so much Monte Carlo noise that you won't be able to diagnose anything.  Give that we're seeing lots of chains getting stuck in initial models with only four chains, it seems like a reasonable choice.

>> Personally I think the best way forward is to improve the adaption.  The first easy fix is to add a period of adaptation-free warmup (which I've been playing with on and off since coming to London but just haven't had time to run significant tests). messages.subject_clean: Boost's uBLAS matrix library does not work with autodiff (example attached)
messages.body_plain:
In an earlier email, Bob outlined the problem:

> The issue with lifespan is that Boost's ublas library for matrices defines static class constants everywhere by wrapping the scalar type. And so does the rosenbrock functions.  This won't work with our variable lifespans. We'd need traits more like those in Eigen, which seem to be modeled on the function-based approach of std::numeric_limits.  I was sort of surprised to see Boost using static constants in ublas --- it's usually bad ju-ju in C++ because of initialization issues.  See:
>
>   /boost/numeric/ublas/matrix.hpp:
>   ----------------------------
>   ...
>   static const value_type one_;

The result of uBLAS's use of static constants is that we get a segmentation fault. The attached test, as written, does not seg fault. By accessing any element in the identity matrix (lines 9-12), it will seg fault.

No error messages, no nothing. It all happens before this code executes. It took us a while to figure out how and where the seg fault was coming from, but we found it.

In short, Stan's autodiff library will not work with Boost's uBLAS matrix library.

Daniel

P.S. This means Boost numeric's ODE solvers will not work with Stan. There are other issues to getting those ODE solvers to work.

Daniel

messages.body_plain:
Exactly.  The problem is with static allocation.

I think we could fix this by replacing the static constant
one_ with a call to a static function one().  That's
how a traits-based approach would do it, and that will work
for us as long as nobody calls the function out of turn.
I assume that's what they were talking about in the ublas
package in their comment saying they should use traits
in the vector header file.

It doesn't make sense conceptually in our reverse-mode
auto-diff to have a free-floating value of type
stan::agrad::var.  The use pattern is:

   -- create var instances for inputs to functions
   -- call the function on those instances
   -- calculate a gradient in a backward pass
   -- free memory

And to boot, it's not thread safe (unless you make
the variable stack thread local, and then there are
performance penalties).

The alternative is to somehow manage multiple memory arenas,
with references from var to the relevant arena.  The problem
with that is that the objects are bigger and there's
a dynamic indirection that's not cheap to follow in
the guts of our loop.

Another alternative would be to have long-lived var
instances.  They wouldn't need any auto-diff because
they wouldn't depend on any var values.  The problem is
that I can't figure out how to do that without
making the value and derivative calls virtual, which
I would also rather not do for speed reasons.

Finally, there's the same mixed-type issue as with Eigen.
They wrap the constants for the algorithm up in
member variable instances of the scalar type, which means
more auto-diff variables that should really be double for us.

What this means is that we don't want the one_ value
to even be a variable --- all we need is a double if we
have double by var matrix multiplication.  And seriously,
we don't even need that --- it's probably expression templated
out somewhere because it's a constant!

So it seemed like the easiest thing to do to just
rewrite their solver calling Eigen instead of ublas
and using double instances instead of var types for
constants.

- Bob

We've been working on the design and building some early
prototypes for a new Stan feature that will let you define
systems of ordinary differential equations and build models
based on their solutions (typically measurement error models
to allow parameters of the system to be estimated from data).

The design thinking up to this point (or at least as much
of our discussions as I can remember) is now consolidated
on our Wiki:

https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/wiki/ODE-Integrator-Support

There's a link to the GitHub branch where Daniel and I are
building prototypes.

We've had lots of input already, especially from Andrew Gelman,
Michael Betancourt, Ben Goodrich and Frederic Bois (Frederic
built MCSim and works with Andrew on pharmacokinetic models).

We'd love to hear any other ideas people might have, so feel
free to comment here on our mailing lists or on the wiki itself.

- Bob

It's not stan-specific, but the standard R parallel library does not
use all available cores by default; it uses 2 (e.g., function
mclapply()).  This can be overridden.   Of course, if you only have 2,
that is all.

leave some headroom for other tasks and b) hyperthreading makes it
appear I have more processors than I really do.

defaults for the parallel library.

messages.subject: separating concerns in RStan (and Stan)
messages.subject_clean: separating concerns in RStan (and Stan)
messages.body_plain:
(This is in response to a feature request I put in for
RStan to separate out a model object.)

The reason to separate model and fit is that they're
different concepts.  The benefit of modularity is
in testing, documentation, and independent use.

I would like to see a model object in R that's a thin
wrapper around the model class in C++.  This is just
used to provide the functions provided by the C++ class.
This is Stan-specific.

A bunch of Markov chains with variable names is a different
concept, and it's independent of how it's generated.  This
concept is not Stan specific.  So I still think it'd be nice
to allow other programs to use the R-hat and n_eff calcs
and nice summary output and graphics.

The fit object for ordinary MCMC sampling would then be a combination of
these two things.   A fit object for optimization could be
something else.  A fit object for variational Bayes could be
yet a different thing.

I do realize this can cause some redundancy in storing
variable names, but I think it's worth it for the separation.
(I don't know if R lets you store references or it it'll just
make a copy;  either way, even a copy of all the names and
dimensions wouldn't be much overhead.)

This is not for RStan 2.0 by the way.  I think it might make most
sense to do this when we add variational inference or a different
kind of sampler, etc.  That'll give us an even better idea of
the functionality we need.

- Bob
